prompt: Why is every problem in NP also in PSPACE?

options.text: Because NP problems can be solved in polynomial time
options.explanation: That's the open P vs NP question. Nobody knows NP problems can be solved in polynomial time.

options.text: Because a polynomial-space machine can try every certificate in turn, reusing the same polynomial space for each check
options.explanation: Correct. Exponentially many certificates take exponential time, but each check needs only polynomial space, which is wiped and reused.
PSPACE allows only polynomial space. That's EXPSPACE.

options.text: It isn't known; NP vs PSPACE is open
options.explanation: Whether NP equals PSPACE is open, but the inclusion of NP in PSPACE is proven.

workedExample:
1. Let V be a polynomial-time verifier whose certificates are at most p(n) bits long.
2. Loop over every possible certificate c in order, using a p(n)-bit counter.
3. For each, run V(x, c). It runs in polynomial time, so it also uses only polynomial space.
4. The space V used is wiped and reused for the next certificate.

```formula
NP ⊆ PSPACE
N_cert < 2^{p(n) + 1}
S = O(p(n)) + q(n)
T ≤ 2^{p(n) + 1}q(n)
where
NP: decision problems whose yes-answers have a short certificate checkable in polynomial time
PSPACE: decision problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory, however long it takes
⊆: "is contained in": every problem on the left is also on the right
n: the input size, in bits
p(n): the polynomial limit on certificate length, in bits
N_cert: the number of certificates of length at most p(n); the geometric sum is below 2 to the power p(n) + 1
q(n): the verifier's polynomial running time, which also bounds the cells it can use
S: the total working memory: the counter plus one verifier run at a time
T: the total running time, in steps
O(...): Big O: at most a constant times this
≤: is at most
In words: try every certificate of length at most p(n) one after another; their count is below two to the power of p(n) plus one. Time multiplies (exponential), but space does not, because each check reuses the same polynomial workspace.
```

5. Time is exponential, space polynomial. Space can be reused; time can't.

prompt: A deterministic machine has 10 states, a binary work alphabet, uses at most 20 work cells, and reads an input of length 1,000. Counting configurations (state, input-head position, work-head position, work-tape contents), how many steps can it run before it **must** have either halted or entered an infinite loop?

options.explanation: That's input length × space and ignores the 2²⁰ possible work-tape contents and the states.
Correct. 10 × 1,000 × 20 × 2²⁰ ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹ configurations. A deterministic machine that runs longer than that repeats a configuration, so it loops forever.
Work-tape contents are only one factor; state and head positions multiply the count.

options.text: There's no bound; it could run for any finite time
options.explanation: With finitely many configurations, a deterministic machine that hasn't halted after visiting more steps than there are configurations has repeated one and will cycle.

workedExample:
1. States: 10.
2. Input-head positions: 1,002, including two end markers.
3. Work-head positions: 20.
4. Work-tape contents: two to the twentieth power, or 1,048,576.

```formula
N_conf = |Q|(n + 2)s|Γ|^s
N_conf = 10 × 1002 × 20 × 2^{20}
N_conf ≈ 2.1 × 10^11
N_conf = 2^{O(s)}   for s ≥ log n
SPACE(s) ⊆ TIME(2^{O(s)})
where
N_conf: the number of distinct configurations (and so the most steps before a repeat)
Q: the set of control states; |Q| = 10 is how many
n: the input length, 1,000 symbols; the read head also has two end-marker positions
s: the work cells used, 20 (work-head positions)
Γ: gamma, the work-tape alphabet; |Γ| = 2 for binary
|Γ|^s: the possible work-tape contents, 2^20 = 1,048,576
log: logarithm base 2
O(s): Big O: at most a constant times s
≈: approximately equal to
SPACE(s): problems a deterministic machine decides in at most a constant times s work cells
TIME(t): problems a deterministic machine decides in at most a constant times t steps
⊆: "is contained in"
In words: about 2.1 × 10^11 configurations, so a deterministic machine still running after that many steps has repeated one and loops forever. In general, space s bounds time by 2 to the power of a constant times s.
```
